name: Academies
lines: A shimmering ward wraps you for 25 seconds and soaks up to 60 harm from any blow: Ironfray's fighters, beasts that ambush you, dreamers where fights are allowed.
A blast of wind in front of you throws back whatever is within 12 m, with a little harm, and the wind at your back speeds you on for 8 seconds.
Whatever is in your hand burns with arcane fire for a minute: every blow and shot of yours does half as much again.
Brew draughts at any Academy cauldron (the Alchemy Laboratory, or Duskwell's laboratory) from herbs you gather. They go in your backpack: drink one from there, or from the Potions button.
Out in any world, find a herb of that land growing near you (the deep has glowcap and pearlmoss, hot lands emberroot, the night moonmint). It goes in your backpack.
The nearest beast that is after you, within 16 m, loses its anger for 30 seconds and wanders off. It does not work on dreamers.
For 30 seconds a mark shows over every dreamer, fighter and beast within 150 m, through walls and rock, and you are told how dangerous this world is.
Burn a glowing rune where you stand. Anywhere else in that world, press it again to have the pointer lead you back to it, or press it on the rune to move it.
Step in an instant to where you are looking, up to 12 m (never through a wall). Fighters and beasts lose sight of you.
An image of you stays where you stand for 12 seconds. Fighters and beasts go for it instead of you.
Your eyes take the dark: caves, the deep, the Sunless Sea and night all show clearly. Switch it on and off.
Cut a ring of sigils 8 m across round where you stand. For 45 seconds no beast or fighter can cross it, and you are told when a dreamer does.
A wisp of starlight follows at your shoulder and lifts the dark round you. Switch it on and off.
Your skin turns to stone for 18 seconds: blows do less than half their harm, but you walk a little slower.
Turn the foe you face (up to 18 m) into a harmless toad for 6 seconds: it cannot fight or chase you. Against a dreamer it strikes hard instead (12).
Call falling stars down on the foe you face, or 14 m ahead: everything within 5 m of where they land is hurt badly (24) and knocked down.
Melt into the shadows and come out at the back of the foe you face (up to 20 m), striking for 22. Never through a wall.
Pour darkness round you, 6 m across, for 8 seconds: you cannot be seen, and everything caught in it is blinded for 2 seconds and hurt.
Curse the foe you face (up to 22 m): it withers for 10 seconds, losing 6 every 2 seconds and dragging its feet. Dreamers wither too.
Let the dark look out of your eyes: every foe within 12 m is hurt (8) and beasts and fighters flee in terror for 5 seconds. Dreamers take 12.
Tear the life out of the foe you face (up to 22 m): 16 harm to it, and the same mended in you.
Sing the stone open: spikes of rock burst from the ground in a line 14 m ahead of you, hurting everything in the way (22) and throwing it down for 2 seconds.
Venomous shadow-silk flies where you look and holds the first foe it meets (up to 18 m) for 4 seconds, its poison biting 5 every second while it holds.
Raise a wraith from the dark for 20 seconds. It hunts the nearest foe within 16 m of you and claws it for 9 every second and a half.
A soap bubble holds its shape because its skin pulls inward evenly all round: the same pull everywhere makes a perfect sphere.
An arcane ward is that skin made of your attention: picture the bubble round you, even on every side, before you need it.
A ward soaks harm until it is spent, then breaks. Cast it before the blow, not after.
Why is a soap bubble round?
Its skin pulls inward evenly on every side
Air inside is heavier than outside
Soap is round by nature
Wind is air moving from high pressure to low. The bigger the difference, the stronger it blows.
To call a gust, picture the air in front of you emptied, and the air behind you rushing to fill it.
Stand side-on and push with both hands: the gust goes where your palms face.
Which way does wind blow?
From high pressure to low pressure
From low pressure to high pressure
Always from the north
A blacksmith quenches hot steel in water so it cools fast: the metal's tiny crystals lock hard. That is why tempered blades hold an edge.
An enchantment is a temper of a different kind: the rune you trace locks a little of your will into the thing in your hand.
It fades as it is used. Enchant just before the fight, never the night before.
Why is hot steel quenched in water?
Cooling it fast locks its crystals hard
Water makes steel shiny
To wash off the soot
Many real medicines began as plants: willow bark gave us aspirin, foxglove a heart medicine. Dose is everything: the same leaf can heal or harm.
An alchemist measures. Every recipe on the lab wall says exactly how much of each herb it takes.
Stir clockwise to bind, counter-clockwise to settle, and never taste what you have not finished.
Which tree's bark led to aspirin?
Plants grow where their needs are met: sun-lovers on open hillsides, shade plants under trees, mosses where it is damp.
Read the land and you know what grows there: the deep grows glowing fungus, hot lands tough roots, and some leaves open only at night.
Take a little from each plant and leave the rest, so it grows back.
Where would a moss most likely grow?
Somewhere damp and shady
An angry animal is usually a frightened one: its heart races and its body gets ready to fight or flee.
Calming is slowing that heart. Lower your eyes, breathe slowly, and let your voice be low and even.
Never corner a beast you are calming. Leave it a way to walk off.
What is an angry animal most often feeling?
Bats find their way in the dark by echolocation: they call out and listen to the echoes coming back off everything around them.
Scrying calls out the same way, with the mind: every living thing near you answers, and you see where it stands, through walls and rock.
The farther you reach, the fainter the answer. A hundred and fifty metres is as far as most scryers can hold.
How do bats find their way in the dark?
They listen to the echoes of their own calls
They see in infrared
They follow the smell of the moon
Sailors and walkers once piled stones into cairns to mark a path: anyone coming after could find the way.
A waymark rune is a cairn of light. Burn it into the ground, and it calls you back from anywhere in that land.
One rune at a time: burn a new one and the old one fades.
A pile of stones marking a path
Light crosses a room faster than you can blink: a blink takes about a tenth of a second.
Blinking is the step taken in that tenth of a second: see where you will stand, and be there.
You can only blink to where you can see. A wall stops the step as it stops your eye.
About how long does a blink of the eye take?
About a tenth of a second
About five seconds
Your eye can be fooled: a still shape the right size in a dim place reads as a person, because the brain fills in what it expects.
A mirror double is an image of you, left standing where you were. Foes see you there, and strike at it.
It lasts a dozen heartbeats. Be gone before they notice.
Why does a still shape in the dark look like a person?
The brain fills in what it expects to see
Eyes see better in the dark
Your eye has rods for dim light and cones for colour. Rods need about twenty minutes in the dark to reach full strength.
Darksight is the patience of the rods, taken all at once: the dark gives up its shapes.
Bright light undoes it in a moment.
Which cells of the eye see in dim light?
A ward was once a thread across a doorway, or a dust of chalk: it showed when something crossed.
A sigil of warding is a ring of runes that says no. Cut it round you and nothing that hunts you can step over it.
It holds for about three quarters of a minute. Do not leave the ring if you want it to keep you.
What did an old ward of chalk show?
That something had crossed it
Where treasure was buried
Starlight that reaches you tonight left its star years ago, some of it thousands of years ago.
The starlight wisp is a little of that old light, called down to follow at your shoulder.
It is gentle on purpose: a bright light would spoil the eyes of everyone near you.
Starlight you see tonight left its star when?
Years ago, sometimes thousands
Basalt is rock made when lava cools quickly: dense, hard and dark. Much of the ocean floor is basalt.
Stoneskin borrows that hardness for your skin. Blows that would cut you only bruise you.
Stone is heavy: you walk slower while it holds. Let it go when the danger has passed.
How is basalt made?
Lava cooling quickly
Sand pressed by the sea
Shells piled up for ages
A caterpillar becomes a butterfly by metamorphosis: inside the chrysalis its body is broken down and built again.
Polymorph forces that change on a foe for a few heartbeats, into the smallest, mildest shape: a toad.
A toad cannot fight. Use the moment to get away, or to deal with the others.
What is it called when a caterpillar becomes a butterfly?
A shooting star is a speck of space rock burning up as it rushes into the air, often no bigger than a grain of sand.
Starfall calls bigger ones down, on purpose, onto one spot.
Mark the spot first: everything near where they land is struck, so never call them on yourself.
What is a shooting star?
A speck of space rock burning up in the air
A star falling from the sky
Owls hunt in near silence: soft fringes on their feathers break up the sound of their wings, so prey never hears them coming.
Shadow Strike is the owl's way: you go into the dark, and come out behind the one you hunt.
Strike once and be ready: the dark hides you only on the way in.
Why can an owl fly almost silently?
Soft fringes on its feathers break up the sound
It holds its breath
It flies very slowly
Octopus and squid squirt a cloud of ink when hunted: the predator loses them in the dark and they slip away.
The Veil of Night is that ink, made of shadow: pour it round you and nothing sees in or out.
Whatever is caught inside it is blind for a moment. Use it to strike or to vanish.
Why does a squid squirt ink?
To hide in the cloud and escape
To glow in the dark
Doctors know the 'nocebo' effect: someone told a harmless pill will hurt them can truly start to feel ill.
A hex of withering does not wait to be believed. It takes hold of the one you curse, and drains them a little at a time.
It cannot be shaken off quickly. Curse first, then keep your distance.
What is the nocebo effect?
Feeling ill because you expect to
Fear lives in a small part of the brain called the amygdala: it sets the heart racing and readies the body to fight or run.
Dread reaches into that part of every foe near you at once, and tells it to run.
Fear passes in a few heartbeats. Strike while they flee.
Which part of the brain is most linked with fear?
Leeches and vampire bats feed on blood, and both make a chemical that stops the blood from clotting while they drink.
Soul Drain drinks deeper than blood: the strength you tear out of a foe flows into you.
It takes as much as it gives. The stronger your foe, the more they feel it.
What does a leech make to keep blood flowing?
A chemical that stops clotting
Sound travels through rock about fifteen times faster than through air, and an earthquake is the rock itself ringing.
Earthrend sings the rock open in a line ahead of you: it bursts upward in spikes.
Aim along the ground. Everything standing in the line is struck and thrown down.
How fast does sound travel through rock, compared with air?
About fifteen times faster
Spider silk is one of the toughest things in nature: for its weight it is stronger than steel and stretches without snapping.
Venom-silk is spun from the dark and soaked in spider venom. It holds the first thing it touches, and bites.
It holds for a few heartbeats, and the venom bites every one of them.
For its weight, how strong is spider silk?
Stronger than steel
As strong as glass
Bones keep their story for thousands of years: scientists can tell from a skeleton how old someone was, what they ate, even how they lived.
A wraith is the shadow of the long dead, raised for a few heartbeats to serve the one who called it.
It hunts what is nearest you. When its time ends it sinks back into the dark.
What can scientists learn from an old skeleton?
How old the person was and how they lived
Their favourite song
Their name, written on the bones

Dim the lamps to half
